claims.text: Adding a controlled low-volume fraction of SiC nanoparticles to MnNiSi-based alloys improves mechanical performance.
SiC nanoparticles improve mechanical performance through dispersion strengthening.
Adding no more than 5 vol.% SiC nanoparticles does not significantly degrade the magnetocaloric effect.
The intervention is to introduce SiC nanoparticles at a volume fraction of 5% or less during MnNiSi-alloy processing.
The nanoparticles must be uniformly dispersed for the hypothesis to hold.
Melt-spinning or powder metallurgy can be used to incorporate the SiC nanoparticles.
Uniformly dispersed SiC nanoparticles will be located both along grain boundaries and within the MnNiSi-based matrix.
Dispersed SiC nanoparticles act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the hardness of the alloy.
Dispersion strengthening by SiC nanoparticles increases the fracture toughness of the alloy.
SiC nanoparticles are chemically inert in the proposed MnNiSi-based material.
The chemical inertness of SiC minimizes interference with the magnetic lattice responsible for the magnetocaloric effect.
Samples containing 2–5 vol.% SiC will show a statistically significant improvement in hardness and/or fracture toughness relative to an additive-free control.
Samples containing no more than 5 vol.% SiC will retain magnetic entropy change similar to that of the additive-free baseline.
SiC contents above approximately 5 vol.% may disrupt magnetic interactions and degrade magnetocaloric performance.
Non-uniform SiC dispersion may disrupt magnetic interactions and degrade magnetocaloric performance.
No direct evidence is available here for SiC-nanoparticle addition to MnNiSi-based systems.
The hypothesis extrapolates from general dispersion-strengthening principles rather than cited MnNiSi-specific evidence.
